title: Maxwell's Equations and Light as a Wave

cards.b:
In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a few equations that gathered all of electricity and magnetism into one theory. Out of the maths popped a surprise: waves of electric and magnetic fields, travelling at a speed equal to the known speed of light.

Maxwell concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. This unlocked radio, television, mobile phones and Wi-Fi.

Maxwell's equations (1865, refining earlier work) say in words:

  1. Gauss's law: electric charges are the source of electric field lines.
  2. No monopoles: magnetic field lines never begin or end; they loop.
  3. Faraday's law: a changing magnetic field makes an electric field.
  4. Ampere-Maxwell law: currents and changing electric fields make magnetic fields.

The last fix, Maxwell's addition of the changing electric field term, was the key to waves.

Here is the idea. A changing magnetic field produces an electric field (Faraday). A changing electric field produces a magnetic field (Maxwell's addition). So a wiggling field can create a second wiggling field, which creates the first, and the pattern runs off through space by itself.

That is an electromagnetic wave: electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. It needs no medium. This is how sunlight crosses empty space.

cards.h: The speed of light drops out
cards.b:
Maxwell's equations contain two constants measured in simple electric and magnetic experiments. Combine them and the wave speed is:

Wave speed

c = 1 / square root of (mu0 x epsilon0) = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s

This matched the measured speed of light so closely that Maxwell concluded: light is an electromagnetic wave. In vacuum, it travels 300,000 km every second, and the Sun's light reaches us in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

In 1887 Heinrich Hertz generated and detected radio waves in his laboratory, confirming Maxwell. The unit of frequency, the hertz, honours him.

Light is only a thin slice of a huge family, the electromagnetic spectrum. From long to short wavelength: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. All obey c = f x wavelength; only the frequency differs.

• Radio: broadcasting, mobile networks.
  • Microwaves: ovens (they shake water molecules), radar, satellite links.
  • Infrared: heat, remote controls, night vision.
  • Visible: what our eyes see, 400 to 700 nanometres.
  • Ultraviolet: sunburn; sterilising.
  • X-rays: pass through flesh; used in medicine.
  • Gamma rays: from nuclei; the most energetic and penetrating.

An FM station broadcasts at 100 MHz (100 million hertz). Wavelength = c / f = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 10 to the power 8 = 3 m.

A mobile phone signal at 900 MHz: wavelength = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 9 x 10 to the power 8 = 0.33 m.

Green light of wavelength 550 nm has frequency = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 5.5 x 10 to the power -7 = 5.5 x 10 to the power 14 Hz, hundreds of trillions of oscillations per second.

• 'Radio waves and light are different things.' Same kind of wave, just different frequency.
  • 'Microwave ovens are radioactive.' Microwaves are non-ionising radio-type waves; they heat food but do not make it radioactive.
  • 'Light needs air to travel.' Electromagnetic waves travel best in vacuum; sound is the one that needs a medium.

cards.h: J. C. Bose and the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope
cards.b:
Jagadish Chandra Bose showed millimetre-wavelength radio waves in Calcutta in 1895 and built early solid-state detectors, years before Marconi's first practical radio transmission; he is often honoured as a pioneer of radio and microwave science.

Today India's Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) near Pune, with 30 dishes, each 45 m across, listens to radio waves from distant galaxies and pulsars. Its design rests on the very same Maxwell's equations.

• Maxwell (1865) unified electricity, magnetism and light.
  • Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other as a travelling wave.
  • c = 3 x 10 to the power 8 m/s; c = f x wavelength.
  • The spectrum runs from radio to gamma rays; Hertz confirmed radio waves in 1887.

Think about it

1. Why can we see the Sun but not hear it?
2. Why can't your mobile phone get a signal in a lift?
